extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Popular Science Monthly; scientifically literate public; publishers and editors of scientific periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and defence of editorial standards for a scientific periodical: what to publish, how to respond to accusations (e.g., of atheism), and what constitutes respectable scientific journalism. Also includes a separate descriptive checklist for evaluating teaching of chemistry and physics in schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'pronounced atheist'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pronounced atheist' must be one who pronounces himself an atheist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine argues that the correct test of whether someone is an atheist is what they profess and teach (i.e., explicit self‑identification), not mere imputation or hostile labeling by opponents. Examples: Bradlaugh may be called a pronounced atheist because he publicly ran for Parliament as one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for charges against the magazine
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations that the magazine 'teaches atheism' require concrete proof (specific passages or evidence) that authors explicitly avow or defend atheism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial rebuttal: the writer in the Post gave as evidence only that the magazine published Herbert Spencer; the magazine contends that this is not proof because Spencer does not avow atheism. Accusers should produce explicit passages showing avowal or defense of atheism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial purpose: publish important scientific results, not polemical pugilism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monthly was established to place before American readers the most important results of scientific thought as presented by its ablest expositors, not to seek polemical or sensational content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference given to valuable scientific articles that are 'too heavy' or excluded from more popular magazines. Editorial policy should prioritize substance and the advancement of scientific understanding over sensationalism or partisan polemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sacrificing character for pecuniary success
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not compromise the intellectual or scientific character of the periodical merely to increase sales or appeal to popular prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a steady editorial course; reject sensational papers whose primary aim is to shock or sell rather than to further scientific understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful, tolerant treatment of religious subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of religious errors is legitimate, but it must be sincere, respectful, and not wantonly irritating or spiteful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish trenchant but respectful analysis from 'spiteful, ruthless, and exasperating assault' upon religious sentiment. The magazine should avoid publishing material intended solely to startle or shock religious readers for sordid purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth, independence, and catholicity of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The periodical should reflect the breadth, independence, and catholicity of contemporary scientific thought, publishing a variety of important perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make room for varied authors (including those of differing views) when possible; use supplements or reprinting channels if space is limited. Aim to represent scientific movements such as evolution where they are central to contemporary discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful representation of scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial policy must represent the progress of scientific thought as faithfully as possible and should not be constrained by doctrinal censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science cannot be edited to please theological objections; the magazine's duty is to reflect evolving scientific knowledge (e.g., studies on species, antiquity of man, brain function, social growth) even if this upsets those who prioritize theological over scientific teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science's role: destroy ignorance and error, not faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Science aims to remove ignorance and error; it is not an enemy of religion per se, and scientific inquiry should not be characterized as intentionally destructive of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where faith opposes truth will science appear as an enemy; otherwise science is the 'best friend of faith' because it seeks enduring foundations for belief. Editors should resist charges that scientific reporting is inherently 'infidel' in motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical and factual accuracy / correction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication should correct typographical errors and factual misstatements when they are detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example correction shown for membership counts: publish explicit errata/corrections (e.g., correct dashes and counts) and explain cause (miscounting from state-of-origin). Promptly publish corrections in subsequent issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological authenticity requires expert confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of authentic inscribed archaeological objects must be evaluated by recognized experts and institutions; authenticity greatly increases the importance of an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit opinions from relevant authorities (e.g., museum curators, Smithsonian specialists, anthropological section judges). If objects are frauds, archaeological specialists should pursue and convict fraud; otherwise publish expert confirmations to validate importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report checklist for teaching chemistry and physics
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating instruction in chemistry and physics, gather specific information on courses of study, textbooks used, apparatus, library facilities and policy, examinations, and cultivation of original research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professor Clarke's report digests replies to a schedule covering these items, and the prefatory chapters offer criticisms and suggested remedies. Use this checklist to state facts and to point out defects and improvements in science instruction at all school grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection: publish valuable work excluded elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Give space to valuable scientific articles that other current magazines exclude because they are 'too heavy', unprofitable, or conflict with public prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial discretion to support the advancement of science by publishing substantial scholarship even if it is not commercially lucrative; supplements may be used to increase available space.
